John Kent
jon kent
proper noun
English surname Kent, from the ancient county; the given name John from Hebrew Yochanan, “the LORD is gracious.”

See also: John Kent

📖 Biblical Definition

John Kent (1766–1843) was a Devonshire shipwright who, unschooled in the academies yet deeply taught in the school of grace, poured out some of the most God-exalting hymnody the Particular Baptists produced. Labouring at Plymouth Dock with his hands, he laboured also in the sanctuary of his heart, and his Gospel Hymns breathe an unashamed sovereign-grace theology: election, particular redemption, the everlasting covenant, and the immutable love of the Father are not merely doctrines he confessed but the very marrow of his song. “Sovereign grace o’er sin abounding” remains his most enduring line, and in it we hear the whole system of the gospel compressed into praise. Kent did not sentimentalize the cross; he magnified it as the ground of the believer’s security, tracing salvation back to the counsel of God before the world began and forward to the glory that shall not fade. He wrote as one who knew himself a debtor to mercy alone, and his verse invites the trembling saint to rest wholly upon a finished work. That a working man with hammer and adze should leave the church such treasure is itself a testimony that the LORD hides these things from the wise and reveals them unto babes, and that the Spirit is no respecter of learning where He purposes to give a singing heart.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

English Particular Baptist hymnwriter (1766–1843) whose sovereign-grace hymns magnify electing love and the everlasting covenant.

expand to see more

A Devonshire shipwright and self-taught hymnwriter among the Particular Baptists.

Author of the collection Gospel Hymns, marked throughout by high Calvinistic doctrine.

Best known for “Sovereign grace o’er sin abounding,” a hymn of the everlasting covenant.

A layman whose verse magnified election, particular redemption, and the immutable love of God.

A witness that saving song may flow from the workbench as truly as from the pulpit.

📖 Key Scripture

Eph 1:4 — "According as he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and without blame before him in love:"

Rom 5:20 — "Moreover the law entered, that the offence might abound. But where sin abounded, grace did much more abound:"

2Sa 23:5 — "Although my house be not so with God; yet he hath made with me an everlasting covenant, ordered in all things, and sure: for this is all my salvation, and all my desire, although he make it not to grow."

Psa 89:2 — "For I have said, Mercy shall be built up for ever: thy faithfulness shalt thou establish in the very heavens."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

A faithful witness, not a contested doctrine; his life recovers the principle of sovereign grace magnified in worship.

expand to see more

John Kent is preserved not because his name is disputed but because his song refuses the age its two favourite errors: that grace is a reward for the willing and that worship is a mood we manufacture. Kent sang the covenant as a thing settled in eternity, and such singing rebukes every gospel that makes the sinner the first cause of his own salvation.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that congregational praise must be doctrinally weighty—that the church sings her theology and so preaches to herself. Where hymnody is drained of election, atonement, and covenant, it becomes flattery of the worshipper rather than adoration of the LORD. Kent’s verse calls us back to a praise that is Godward, cross-centred, and grounded in immutable love.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Kent’s hymnody roots the church’s worship in the eternal covenant of grace and the doctrines of sovereign mercy.

expand to see more

The everlasting covenant, “ordered in all things, and sure,” as the theme of praise (2Sa 23:5).

Election unto holiness before the foundation of the world (Eph 1:4).

The superabounding of grace over the abounding of sin (Rom 5:20).

The mercy that is “built up for ever” and cannot fail the saints (Psa 89:2).

The dignity of lay labour offered up in worship as a fragrant sacrifice of song.

Usage

"“We closed the Lord’s Supper singing Kent’s ‘Sovereign grace o’er sin abounding.’”"

"“His hymns teach a whole doctrine of the covenant in four stanzas.”"

"“A shipwright by trade, John Kent left the church a treasury of sovereign-grace praise.”"
